# Appeal of Adverse Benefit Determination — Reference POC-A5F6D22435-38075

**To:** Security Health Plan, Member Appeals Department
**From:** Rowan Brooks, Member ID W772624569
**Re:** Denial dated 2026-08-07 of Total Hip Replacement (CPT 27130) — Reference POC-A5F6D22435-38075
**Governing policy cited:** eviCore CMM-311/312/313/314/315/601/606/609 series (generic EviCore editions, same URLs as WellSense entry), Comprehensive Musculoskeletal Management Guidelines V2.0.2025, https://www.evicore.com/sites/default/files/clinical-guidelines/2025-08/EviCore_CMM-311%20Knee%20Replacement%20Arthroplasty_V2.0.2025_Eff11.05.2025_upd08.12.2025.pdf

Dear Security Health Plan,

I am asking you to reconsider the denial of my total hip replacement surgery (CPT 27130), which was denied in a notice dated 2026-08-07, reference number POC-A5F6D22435-38075. My surgeon, Dr. Lindqvist, has documented that this surgery is medically necessary, and I believe the record supports that conclusion.

## Why I am appealing

The denial states that "the imaging findings submitted do not support the medical necessity of the requested procedure." I want to walk through what is actually in my record and how it lines up with the plan's own published clinical criteria.

**My symptoms and function.** I have had progressive hip pain for 24 months that is not relieved by rest. I now walk with a cane, am limited to about one block, and cannot put on my shoes unassisted. On exam, provocative testing was positive on the affected side and my range of motion is limited by pain.

**My imaging.** A weight-bearing AP pelvis radiograph taken 2026-06-09 showed joint space narrowed to 1 mm superolaterally, with subchondral sclerosis and osteophytes — findings consistent with advanced degenerative joint disease.

**My conservative treatment.** I completed 16 weeks of supervised physical therapy focused on hip abductor strengthening and gait (2026-02-22 through 2026-06-14, 16 visits), documented in my physical therapy discharge note. I also took NSAIDs for 6 months without adequate relief, and had a corticosteroid injection on 2026-03-29 that gave only about 3 weeks of partial relief. I have no active infection, no untreated substance use, a BMI of 29, and I do not smoke.

## How this measures against the plan's own guideline language

The guideline document the plan applies to joint replacement review defines non-surgical management this way:

> "Non-Surgical Management (with regard to the treatment of lower extremity joint pain) any provider-directed non-surgical treatment, which has been demonstrated in the scientific literature as efficacious and/or is considered reasonable care in the treatment of lower extremity joint pain."

My physical therapy, NSAID trial, and corticosteroid injection are exactly this kind of provider-directed, evidence-based non-surgical treatment, and they were tried and documented before my surgeon recommended surgery.

The same guideline document also states:

> "The medical record must clearly document why provider-directed non-surgical management is not appropriate."

In my case, the record does not need to show that non-surgical management was inappropriate — it shows that non-surgical management was tried in full (16 weeks of PT, 6 months of NSAIDs, and an injection) and failed to give lasting relief, alongside imaging that documents advanced joint space narrowing and sclerosis.

I want to note something for the reviewer: the criteria excerpts available to me from this guideline set are written

evidence.criteria_request: Joint and spine surgery go through eviCore, whose guidelines are public. Security Health also has its own 'Total Hip Replacement Surgery' policy on their PolicyTech site. Note their 'Back Surgical Procedures' and hip impingement policies now redirect to a Sanford Health login - request those in writing.
